extracted.intended_audience: advertising creatives, agency leaders, marketers, and awards jurors
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and practical considerations for creating and evaluating humorous advertising, especially in the context of international awards (e.g., Cannes). Covers translatability, creative craft, client buy-in, timing, and sensitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translatability / physical humour
rubrics_metrics.description: The funny ads that do tend to break through employ physical humour that can easily transcend language barriers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For international awards or global campaigns prefer humour that does not rely on wordplay or local idioms; physical comedy and visual gags travel better across languages and cultures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context-dependence / shared knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour is all about context, so it can be hard to appreciate some jokes without shared knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that culturally-specific references or niche context may not land with diverse juries/audiences; test for whether the required background knowledge is likely to be shared.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of craft / writing quality
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a general lack of recognition of the skill involved in creating something funny. It requires good writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in high-quality writing and comedic craft; judges and audiences reward well-executed humour even if it's subtle. Poorly written jokes undermine effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Client alignment and ability to sell it upwards
rubrics_metrics.description: It requires ... a client that shares a sense of humour and can sell it upwards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure client buy-in early; humour often gets cut or diluted if the client or stakeholders are not aligned. Work on internal advocacy to preserve comedic intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awards bias toward purpose-driven work
rubrics_metrics.description: When trying to choose between a serious, purpose-driven campaign that is claiming to save the world, and an irreverent, funny ad, it may be hard to argue for the one that just makes you chuckle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that juries (especially in the current climate) may favour campaigns with social purpose or cultural relevance; if you want awards recognition, consider how humour can sit alongside meaningful purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity and timing in crises
rubrics_metrics.description: Many brands feel they don’t have permission to be joking around during a tragedy. The polarised nature of the social debate is also probably leading many brands to steer clear of anything that could be interpreted as offensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess cultural tone and timing carefully—during crises or charged political moments humour can be perceived as inappropriate. Prioritise sensitivity and avoid gags that could inflame debate or seem tone-deaf.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour's effectiveness: memorability and cut-through
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour can be extremely effective because it is memorable, cuts through noise and bonds people together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use humour strategically to increase recall and brand affinity; measure success by how well the work is remembered and whether it builds a positive bond with the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty of execution / need for courage
rubrics_metrics.description: Great humour is a dying art, it’s difficult, you need great writing and a client who shares your sense of humour. Being funny requires courage at the best of times and sensitivity too.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that good comedy is hard and risky—teams must be prepared for possible backlash and have the conviction to stand behind well-crafted humour when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Briefing and research limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Maybe that’s why it’s rarely briefed in. Researching humour is tricky too; trying to pull off humour on a 'board-o-matic' is a joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brief humour explicitly in creative briefs and invest in appropriate testing methods; avoid relying solely on static boards or simplistic tests to judge comedic timing or tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Global audience mismatch / lost in translation
rubrics_metrics.description: Put all that on the global stage, and the audience often isn’t sharing the humour, it’s lost in translation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating work for international awards or global distribution, be cautious of humour that depends on local culture; either adapt the joke by market or select universal comedic devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness to the cultural moment
rubrics_metrics.description: The winning work feels appropriate for the year we’ve had but, in my opinion, we still need to have a laugh. The best work ... were reflections of the times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Align tone and subject matter with current socio-cultural realities; humour that resonates because it reflects or comments on the moment is more likely to be embraced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target selection and affectionate tone
rubrics_metrics.description: All humour ultimately makes fun of someone or something, although at its best, in an affectionate way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose targets carefully—punching up or affectionate teasing is safer and more likely to be accepted than mean-spirited or punching-down humour, which risks offense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Levity as emotional relief and bonding
rubrics_metrics.description: We like to describe making someone laugh as shortening the distance between two people ... whether it’s a person or a brand telling the joke, the same principle applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use levity to create fleeting bonds and likability; in difficult times well-placed humour can help audiences cope and remember the brand positively.
